title: Seven Hills Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Seven Hills wells have a 200 ft median depth, 7 gpm median yield, and estimated finished costs of $19,000-$32,000.
h1: Seven Hills, Colorado Well and Drilling Guide
intro_html:
Buying land in Seven Hills means evaluating the well as part of the property, not as an afterthought. The records within five miles include 5,268 permitted wells, but only a portion report both construction details and performance data.

This is mountain ground dominated by fractured-bedrock wells, so nearby results are useful for planning but cannot guarantee what a new hole will produce. Pine Brook Hill, Tall Timber, Crisman, Mountain Meadows, Sunshine, and Lazy Acres provide useful local comparisons when reviewing permits and talking with a driller.

sections.heading: Seven Hills well depth reflects fractured mountain bedrock
sections.html:
The median reported well depth near Seven Hills is 200 feet. The middle half runs from 35 to 380 feet, which is a wide spread for a buyer trying to budget a new well. About 37% of reported wells are under 100 feet, 26% fall between 100 and 300 feet, 28% are between 300 and 600 feet, and 9% exceed 600 feet. The deepest recorded well is 4,550 feet.

Most permits name an unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer: 4,790 wells, compared with 80 alluvial wells and 45 Quaternary Alluvium wells. Fractured granite and gneiss can produce water through isolated cracks, so depth can change sharply from one lot to the next. Ask for neighboring well logs before accepting a fixed drilling assumption.

sections.heading: Most Seven Hills wells make usable household yields
sections.html:
Among the 990 wells that report a pump yield, the median is 7.0 gallons per minute. The middle half is 5.0 to 10.0 gallons per minute, and 70% report yields from 5 to 15 gallons per minute. Another 18% are in the 1-to-5-gallon range, 2% are under 1 gallon per minute, and 9% exceed 15 gallons per minute.

That distribution is generally workable for a household when storage and the pumping system are designed correctly, but a 7.0-gpm median is not a promise for a particular parcel. A buyer should review the actual well test, pump setting, recovery behavior, and permitted use. Household wells are commonly exempt wells, subject to their permit conditions and Colorado water rules.

sections.heading: Water levels vary, with recent records deeper than the overall median
sections.html:
The overall median static water level is 42 feet below the ground surface, with the middle half between 11 and 100 feet. Only 148 records report a static water level, so this is a smaller and less uniform sample than the depth data.

Measurements by decade do not form a steady decline. The median was 32 feet in the 1960s, 40 in the 1970s, 60 in the 1980s, 6 in the 2000s, 78 in the 2010s, and 75 in the 2020s. The recent decade values are deeper than the overall median, but the large swings and limited reporting do not prove that the water table is dropping across Seven Hills. Have a driller measure the existing well and evaluate seasonal behavior.

sections.heading: Permit history shows long use, with drilling still occurring
sections.html:
Seven Hills has a long permit history. Records show 109 permits from the 1950s, 231 from the 1960s, 919 from the 1970s, 619 from the 1980s, 789 from the 1990s, 477 from the 2000s, 373 from the 2010s, and 266 from the 2020s. The newest permit year is 2025.

The records identify Ground Water Systems Inc. (Wilson, Richard R.) on 867 permits, Authorized (Pe, Pg) on 601, and Ingram Drilling Inc. (Ingram, Stephen E.) on 251. These counts describe permit records, not current availability or endorsements. Confirm licensing, insurance, schedule, and the proposed scope directly with any driller. Review the DWR permit, construction report, and well test rather than relying only on a seller’s summary.

sections.heading: Budget about $19,000 to $32,000 for a finished median-depth well
sections.html:
Seven Hills is fractured mountain bedrock, described in the drilling model as granite and gneiss. The typical drilling rate is $65 to $100 per foot. At the 200-foot median depth, the drilled hole models to about $13,000 to $20,000.

A finished well, including the pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical work, models to about $19,000 to $32,000 at that depth. The wide local depth range means a bid based only on the median can be misleading: a hole near 380 feet has a different drilling exposure than one under 100 feet. Get a written bid that explains footage, casing, grout, mobilization, testing, pump equipment, power, trenching, and what happens if the hole is dry or produces too little water.

sections.heading: Check contamination, dry-hole exposure, and the building plan
sections.html:
Environmental screening matters around Seven Hills. Within about 10 miles are 89 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 693 historic mine features, and 67 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Those mapped locations do not establish contamination at a specific parcel, but they are reasons to check site proximity, historic uses, laboratory water tests, and local agency records.

Low yield and dry holes remain practical risks in fractured rock, even where nearby wells perform well. Also confirm separation from septic components, wells, property lines, driveways, and proposed structures before construction. A septic system and house layout can limit the best drilling location. Water quality testing should cover the concerns appropriate to the parcel’s history, and an existing well should be inspected rather than judged by flow alone.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Seven Hills, Colorado?
faq.a: The median reported depth within five miles of Seven Hills is 200 feet. The middle half runs from 35 to 380 feet, while 37% are under 100 feet and 9% exceed 600 feet. The deepest record is 4,550 feet. Because most permits name fractured bedrock, neighboring depths help with planning but cannot predict a specific lot.

faq.q: What does it cost to drill a well in Seven Hills?
faq.a: The local model uses $65 to $100 per foot in fractured granite and gneiss. At the 200-foot median depth, drilling alone is estimated at $13,000 to $20,000. A finished well with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical work is estimated at $19,000 to $32,000. A contractor should price the actual site and explain dry-hole terms.

faq.q: How much water do wells produce in Seven Hills?
faq.a: Of the wells reporting a pump yield, the median is 7.0 gallons per minute and the middle half is 5.0 to 10.0 gallons per minute. About 2% report under 1 gallon per minute, while 70% report 5 to 15 gallons per minute. Request the property’s well test and recovery information before relying on area statistics.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Seven Hills?
faq.a: Permit records do not establish drinking-water safety. The area has 89 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 693 historic mine features, and 67 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites within about 10 miles. Test the actual well, review nearby environmental history, and repeat testing when conditions or ownership change. A mapped site is a reason to investigate, not proof of contamination.

faq.q: Is the water table dropping in Seven Hills?
faq.a: The reported static-water medians vary by decade: 32 feet in the 1960s, 40 in the 1970s, 60 in the 1980s, 6 in the 2000s, 78 in the 2010s, and 75 in the 2020s. Recent measurements are deeper than the overall 42-foot median, but only 148 wells report static levels and the series is irregular. It does not prove a consistent regional decline.
